newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolia PM says economy stable, invites investors.
newsitem.headline: Mongolia PM says economy stable, invites investors.

text.p: Mongolia has pulled its economy out of crisis and hopes to rein in inflation in 1997 to below 45 percent while spurring economic growth to five percent, Prime Minister M. Enkhsaikhan said.

Enkhsaikhan also invited foreign investors to his country, promising investment risks would be minimised. "We have been able to clear up the burning crisis points in areas where they had accumulated in the economy," Enkhsaikhan told Reuters in an interview late on Tuesday.

Speaking six months after his Democratic Union government was elected in polls that ended more than 75 years of rule by the communists and their heirs, Enkhsaikhan said his priorities had been to tackle power shortages and banking problems.
Higher energy prices after the state liberalised prices in September had already made power supplies more reliable by helping power plants to clear their debts and buy coal, he said.
"The financial condition of coal mines and power stations has already improved," said the 42-year-old Enkhsaikhan, who holds a doctorate in economics.
The government last December closed two commercial banks, including Mongolia's largest, to halt losses.
Mounting bad loans by Mongolia's banks had prompted the government to tighten credit, but the bank closures had sparked a turnaround, he said.
"Because of the losses, normal circulation of funds...had gone down," Enkhsaikhan said. "We had to take measures."

The government also planned to issue state debt worth up to 50 billion tugriks ($72.5 million) as part of measures to revive the economy, he said. It issued 300 million tugriks in 90-day debt last October.
The government had set a goal of cutting inflation in 1997 to below 45 percent and boosting gross domestic product growth to above five percent, he said.

"In 1996, (annual) inflation was 56 percent, but in 1997 it will not exceed 40-45 percent," Enkhsaikhan said. "Towards the end of this year it will be kept to about two or three percent on a monthly basis."
The State Statistical Centre said annual inflation in 1996 was 53.2 percent. Preliminary estimates placed economic growth in 1996 at 2.6 percent.
His government also plans to diversify exports, which currently depend on copper and cashmere, leaving Mongolia vulnerable to international price fluctuations.
A 35 percent drop in world copper prices in 1996 had had a direct impact on the economy, he said. He did not give details.
"The government policy for the future is to diversify export items...and in this connection to encourage foreign investment," he said.
"We invite foreign investment to Mongolia. We will create an environment... where risks for any kind of investment would be minimal," he said. He did not elaborate on specific policies.
Major foreign investment was expected to flow into the mining sector, especially oil exploration and mining of gold, copper and silver.
Mongolia also hoped for foreign investment in stocks as it pushed ahead with a wave of privatisations, Enkhsaikhan said.
No lists of state entities to be privatised have yet been published, but all state property nationwide is now being registered for privatisation.
"The year 1997 will be a year of large-scale privatisation," Enkhsaikhan said. "By the year 2000, we plan to have 60 percent of state property privatised."
